issues.legal_issue: Adverse judicial remarks should not be expunged when the affected party had an opportunity to respond, the record supports the remarks, and they were necessary to decide the case.
material_facts: The applications sought to expunge adverse remarks made in an earlier judgment concerning an organisation’s assertions about who had actual physical possession of acquired land.
The organisation had asserted that possession had been taken, relying on affidavits and other records; the State disputed that assertion.

A court-directed inspection and report found that the tenure-holders were in actual physical possession of the land. The organisation’s representative was present during the inspection, and the parties received the report and had an opportunity to object and make submissions.
The earlier decision addressed actual physical possession, rather than whether tenure-holders were justified in retaining possession under a rehabilitation policy.
The Court considered the remarks to be based on the pleadings and relevant to resolving the possession dispute.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to expunge the adverse remarks because the governing considerations for making them had been satisfied; the applications to expunge were not accepted on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: A court has inherent jurisdiction to expunge adverse remarks, but should exercise it only in exceptional cases, where expunging is justified to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice. Under State of U.P. v. Mohammad Naim, AIR 1964 SC 703, relevant considerations include whether the person concerned was before the court or could explain their conduct, whether evidence on the record supported the remarks, and whether comment on that conduct was necessary to decide the case. The Court noted that this approach had been followed in Jage Ram, Inspector of Police v. Hans Raj Midha; R.K. Lakshmanan v. A.K. Srinivasan; Niranjan Patnaik v. Sashibhusan Kar; Major General I.P.S. Dewan v. Union of India; Dr. Dilip Kumar Deka v. State of Assam; and State of Maharashtra v. Public Concern for Governance Trust.

rule.if: application_to_expunge_judicial_remarks and affected_person_had_opportunity_to_respond and record_supported_the_remarks and remarks_were_necessary_to_decide_case

predicates.application_to_expunge_judicial_remarks: A party applies to have adverse judicial remarks about its conduct removed.
predicates.affected_person_had_opportunity_to_respo: The person or organisation criticised was before the court or had an opportunity to explain or defend its conduct.
predicates.record_supported_the_remarks: Evidence or pleadings in the record supported the observations about the conduct.
predicates.remarks_were_necessary_to_decide_case: The observations about the conduct were necessary to resolve the controversy before the court.

issues.definition: When an application seeks removal of judicial remarks and the affected person could respond, the record supports the remarks, and they were necessary to decide the case, the remarks are not expunged.

issues.legal_issue: Criticism of a public-interest organisation should be framed with regard to its work for vulnerable beneficiaries while preserving safeguards requiring responsible pleadings and disclosure.
material_facts: The organisation had represented poor and vulnerable oustees in public-interest proceedings.
The Court maintained its finding that the organisation had not taken appropriate pleadings and had not acted with sufficient responsibility.
Counsel submitted that the organisation had served poor farmers over many years and expressed remorse, acknowledging that it should have acted more responsibly.

The Court modified the relevant paragraph to balance the interests of the parties and direct that future presentations by the organisation be considered cautiously, with insistence on proper pleadings, full and fair disclosure, and an affidavit from a responsible person.
issues.conclusion: The Court modified the relevant paragraph to retain criticism of the organisation’s conduct while directing cautious consideration of its future presentations and requiring proper pleadings, full and fair disclosure, and supporting affidavits from responsible persons.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial observations should be guided by justice, fair play, and restraint. In balancing the interests involved in public-interest litigation, the court may take account of the poverty, limited ability to articulate claims, illiteracy, backwardness, and lack of awareness of the people represented, while requiring responsible pleading and truthful disclosure. The Court’s approach to restraint in making adverse observations draws on State of U.P. v. Mohammad Naim, AIR 1964 SC 703.

predicates.public_interest_case_involves_vulnerable: An organisation presents claims in a public-interest case on behalf of people who are poor, marginalised, or otherwise limited in their ability to present their own claims.
predicates.representative_made_inadequate_pleadings: The organisation did not present the facts in adequate pleadings or with the required full and fair disclosure.
predicates.representative_acknowledged_need_for_gre: The organisation or its counsel expressed remorse or acknowledged that it should have acted more responsibly.

issues.definition: When a public-interest representative acts for vulnerable beneficiaries, submits inadequate pleadings, and acknowledges the need for greater responsibility, its future presentations are subject to careful scrutiny and proper disclosure requirements.
